finding.claim: The /mirror endpoint fetches a caller-supplied URL. The only check is host.endswith('example.com'), with no leading dot, so any attacker-registered domain ending in 'example.com' (for example attackerexample.com) passes. The attacker can point such a domain at internal IPs, such as 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1, or at their own server. The intended ALLOWED_SUFFIX = '.example.com' is defined but never used. There is also no scheme restriction, no IP or DNS-rebinding check, and no port restriction.
finding.source: `url` query parameter of GET /mirror (mirror.py:11), supplied by any unauthenticated HTTP client

trace.note: url taken directly from the query string
weak check: host.endswith('example.com') matches evil-example.com, attackerexample.com and similar; the dot-prefixed ALLOWED_SUFFIX (line 7) is unused
c.get(url) issues the server-side request to the attacker-chosen host

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is the endswith check at line 13, which is bypassable. ALLOWED_SUFFIX is unused. There is no scheme allowlist, no resolved-IP check against private or link-local ranges, and no authentication. httpx does not follow redirects by default, so redirect-based bypass is not a factor. The response body is not returned, only len(r.text), which limits impact to blind SSRF and a response-size oracle. The request is still sent, so internal GET endpoints can be triggered and internal services probed.

verdict.guard_found: Only host.endswith("example.com") at mirror.py:13 (suffix check, bypassable); ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused; no auth, scheme, or IP checks; no middleware in the single-file app.
verdict.reason: mirror.py:11 takes the unauthenticated `url` query param, mirror.py:13 only does a suffix endswith("example.com") that attackerexample.com passes, and mirror.py:16 issues httpx get(url) with no closing guard (blind SSRF, since only len(r.text) is returned at line 17).
